chapterOverview.guidingQuestion: How do humans change the planet?
chapterOverview.purpose: The goal for this component idea is for students to explore ways that humans change areas on and near Earth's surface which also affect other Earth systems. The changes caused by humans affect the course of human civilizations. Across the Earth and Human Activity (ESS3) chapters, students explore how Earth's processes affect human societies and how human activities, in turn, influence Earth's systems. ESS3.C focuses on human impacts on Earth systems.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: Throughout history, human actions have had effects on Earth's systems. Individuals can take actions to reduce their impact on Earth's systems. As humans began to form communities, their effects on the environment became larger. Communities can implement systems to reduce their impact on Earth's systems. Humans affect the biosphere as well as other systems, but humans can develop technologies that can reduce as well as remediate past and present changes to Earth's systems.

K-2.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 2. Things that people do to live comfortably can affect the world around them. But they can make choices that reduce their impacts on the land, water, air, and other living things—for example, by reducing trash through reuse and recycling. – NRC, 2012
K-2.progression:
Young learners enter school with many everyday experiences using objects and materials that make life comfortable or convenient. They may choose between drinking from a faucet or a reusable bottle or help adults place items into trash bins. These familiar routines provide a starting point for students to notice that the things people do each day can have effects on their immediate surroundings. At this age, students are not expected to analyze large-scale environmental problems. Instead, the focus is on helping them recognize simple cause-and-effect relationships between their actions and observable changes in the land, water, air, or the living things around them.

Students in this grade band can begin to consider why people use certain materials and how those choices create different kinds of waste. They can explore the idea that people have basic needs, and that many daily conveniences build upon those needs. For example, students may compare the experience of carrying a reusable lunch sack to throwing away a bag each day. Such experiences help them see that it is possible to enjoy comfort and convenience while also reducing negative impacts on their surroundings. Instruction at this level should rely on activities that allow students to observe the effects of their own actions. For example, guided monitoring of classroom or cafeteria trash can help students identify different types of waste and consider ways to reduce particular kinds of trash. Similarly, schoolyard clean-ups or litter inventories can help students see that waste does not disappear and can influence the environment where they live and play.

Instruction should emphasize that individual choices matter, but also that these choices are part of larger patterns of behavior. For instance, separating recyclables requires extra work, yet students can observe the direct results of their efforts. Experiences like these support the idea that their actions matter and connect science content to students' own lives. Teachers can help students make sense of these ideas by asking questions about what they notice when they use certain materials, how much waste they produce, or what happens to items after they are thrown away. These conversations build connections by linking everyday observations to emerging ideas about land, water, air, and living things as interconnected parts of the environment.

These early learning experiences prepare students for the more complex ideas they will encounter in later grades. In upper elementary school, students will consider how communities, not just individuals, influence the environment. They will explore how groups of people living and working together produce larger effects on local resources and environments. In the middle grades, students will learn that larger populations and increased resource use can amplify human impacts at regional or global scales. These later understandings grow naturally from the foundational idea developed in K–2: people make choices that affect their immediate environment, and they can also take actions that reduce those effects.

3-5.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 5. Human activities in agriculture, industry, and everyday life have had major effects on the land, vegetation, streams, ocean, air, and even outer space. But individuals and communities are doing things to help protect Earth's resources and environments. For example, they are treating sewage, reducing the amounts of materials they use, and regulating sources of pollution such as emissions from factories and power plants or the runoff from agricultural activities. – NRC, 2012
3-5.progression:
In earlier grades, students explored familiar actions that individuals take to make life more comfortable and convenient, and they learned that these actions can affect the land, water, air, and living things in their local environment. They also experienced ways that individual choices, such as reusing materials or separating waste, can reduce these effects. These early ideas set the foundation for recognizing that people do not act only as individuals. People live and work together, and groups of people often make similar decisions. As a result, activities that meet the needs of a community can have larger and more noticeable effects on Earth's systems.

In the upper elementary grades, students begin to consider how people act together in organized ways to meet shared needs. They examine how activities such as growing food, obtaining materials, or building structures support communities and make many aspects of life possible. These activities involve groups of people acting at the same time or in the same place, and students can reason that collective actions can cause effects that are greater than the actions of one person alone. For example, students may notice how clearing land for a school garden changes the local area more than a single person's gardening does at home. This helps students recognize that when people work at larger scales, their actions can change environments in both positive and negative ways.

Instruction in this grade band should give students opportunities to connect human activities to observable changes in their surroundings. Students can investigate how groups use land, water, and materials and consider how those uses affect the environment. They should also explore how communities reduce impacts by changing practices or implementing shared solutions, such as improving the use of water or reducing waste. These experiences help students understand that the same kinds of actions that create impacts can also be used to lessen them when people act intentionally.

These ideas prepare students to make sense of more complex patterns in later grades. In the middle grades, students will learn that human impacts grow not only because people work together but also because populations increase and per-capita resource use expands. They will examine how larger-scale activities affect entire ecosystems and the biosphere. The shift from individual actions in the early grades to community-scale actions in grades 3–5 creates a natural progression for understanding how human activities can shape Earth's systems at broader scales.

6-8.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 8. Human activities have significantly altered the biosphere, sometimes damaging or destroying natural habitats and causing the extinction of many other species. But changes to Earth's environments can have different impacts (negative and positive) for different living things. Typically, as human populations and per-capita consumption of natural resources increase, so do the negative impacts on Earth unless the activities and technologies involved are engineered otherwise. – NRC, 2012
6-8.progression:
By middle school, students have developed an understanding that human activities at the scale of individuals and communities can influence the land, water, air, and living things around them. They have also begun to recognize that when groups of people work together or make similar decisions, the combined effects on local environments are larger and more noticeable than the actions of one person alone. These early ideas prepare students to reason about a broader set of patterns in grades 6–8, when human impacts extend beyond local surroundings and begin to shape entire ecosystems and the biosphere.

In this grade band, students consider how human impacts grow not only because more people live on the planet but also because each person uses more resources over time. This understanding connects two related ideas: population size and per-capita consumption. Students examine how human activities such as land development, agriculture, energy use, and material production scale with both the number of people and the amount of energy or material each person uses. They also begin to consider the role of technologies in shaping resource use. Although new technologies often become more efficient over time, greater efficiency does not always lead to lower overall consumption. As technologies become more widely adopted or make certain activities easier or more affordable, total resource use may increase even when individual devices or processes require less energy or material. This helps students understand why human impacts can continue to grow even in the presence of technological improvements.

Instruction in this grade band should help students analyze these patterns using maps, datasets, images, and real-world examples that reveal how human activities alter ecosystems and the biosphere. Students can investigate how changes to land cover, water quality, or habitat availability affect living things, and they can explore why different species experience human impacts in different ways. These investigations allow students to see that human impacts are not uniform. For example, clearing land for agriculture benefits people by providing food, but it can also reduce available habitat for wildlife. Such examples help students recognize that the same action can have both positive and negative consequences depending on the part of the environment being considered.

Teachers can support coherence across the curriculum by connecting these ideas to students' understanding of Earth's systems from ESS2 and to their developing knowledge of energy and matter transformations from physical science. Students can trace how materials and energy move through ecosystems, and then analyze how human activities alter these flows. These connections strengthen students' ability to reason about environmental changes in terms of mechanisms and system interactions, rather than isolated events.

These middle-grade understandings set the stage for the more complex ideas encountered in high school. Students will eventually examine how human activities affect Earth systems at regional and global scales, including atmospheric composition, climate, and biodiversity. They will also explore how societies manage resources, design technologies, and coordinate policies to reduce impacts. The foundational ideas developed in grades 6–8, especially the relationship between population, per-capita consumption, and the scaling of impacts, prepare students to evaluate the sustainability of human activities and consider how multiple solutions can work together to mitigate global effects.

columns.label: Types of Activities That Impact Earth Systems

table.typesOfActivities: Individual actions for comfort and convenience.
table.mitigationActions: Individuals can make decisions to lessen their impacts.

table.typesOfActivities: Community scale activities that support shared living.
table.mitigationActions: Communities can act together to protect resources and environments.

progression.narrative:
Across the grade bands, students deepen their understanding of how human activities influence Earth systems and how people can act to reduce these impacts.

In early grades, students consider the effects of everyday decisions that they make to be more comfortable or convenient. These experiences help them recognize that personal choices, such as using reusable lunch bags, putting trash in trash cans, or conserving resources by turning off lights, can decrease or increase their impact on the environment.

By upper elementary school, students consider how people live and work together in communities, where shared activities such as transportation, food production, and building homes shape the surrounding environment. At this stage, students also learn that communities can act collectively to protect resources and improve environmental conditions by doing things like monitoring pollution from factories or agriculture.

In the middle grades, students extend their thinking beyond individual and community actions and consider how population growth and increasing resources use scale human impacts across ecosystems and the biosphere. They learn that the magnitude of these impacts depends on the number of people and also how societies use materials, energy, and technology. Students also explore how engineered solutions and intentional decision-making can reduce or prevent impacts from increasing in proportion to human activity.

By high school, students are ready to reason about human activities that operate at regional to global scales, including changes to atmospheric composition, water availability, and biodiversity. They examine how impacts accumulate over time and affect the sustainability of human societies. Students also analyze how coordinated innovations, resource management practices, and policies, for example international agreements, can mitigate global environmental impacts and in some cases reverse damaging trends.

standards.statement: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact from humans on land, water, air, and other living things in the local environment.
standards.bigIdea: People do things each day that affect the land, water, air, and other living things where they live. They can make choices that reduce those effects.
scientificIdeas: People have needs and do things that meet these needs more easily or comfortably (e.g., Pre-packaged lunches take less time to prepare than packing a lunch).
Many everyday actions have effects on land, water, air, or the things living nearby (e.g., placing trash in bins keeps materials out of places where animals live).
Human actions add materials to the environment where it's not usually found (e.g., bits of tires end up along the sides of highways).
Air and water can carry materials, so things people leave on the ground may end up in other places.
People can choose to use materials in ways that make less trash (e.g., reducing packaging or using reusable spoons).
commonStudentIdeas: Humans only affect the environment when they do "big" things (e.g., building a house).
As long as people pick up their trash, they are not affecting the environment.
Trash disappears/breaks down/goes away after it's thrown away.
Items that blow away or wash away are gone and don't become part of the environment.
The only acceptable solutions are those that completely eliminate trash or impacts.

standards.statement: Engage in an argument, using evidence from research, that human activity (e.g., farming, mining, building) can affect the land and ocean in positive and/or negative ways.
standards.bigIdea: When people work together to meet their common needs, their activities can have positive or negative effects. These effects become more noticeable as more people make similar decisions.
scientificIdeas: Human effects often occur at scales larger than one person acting alone (e.g., growing food, building structures).
When many people make the same decisions, the combined effects on the environment are greater than the effects of a single individual.
Humans working together can have positive effects on the environment (e.g., habitat restoration, cleaning up shorelines).
Human activities can negatively affect Earth's systems (e.g., removing habitat, changing landforms, introducing new materials in waterways).
Many activities have mixed effects. For example, growing food supports communities, but introduces larger scale changes to land.
Larger-scale activities may have more observable evidence of their impacts that could be gathered from a variety of sources (e.g., maps, satellite images, simple datasets, firsthand accounts).
commonStudentIdeas: The ocean and land are so large that human activities cannot significantly change them.
Human activities are either entirely good or entirely bad.
Human impact only refers to "bad things" caused by people.
Activities only affect the place where they happen, and not nearby land or waterways.
Activities that help people cannot have negative effects.

standards.statement: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the impacts of human activities on the biosphere including conservation, habitat management, species endangerment, and extinction.
standards.bigIdea: Growing human populations and emerging technologies can alter ecosystems and the biosphere in ways that benefit some species and harm others. People can take actions to reduce or counteract these effects.
scientificIdeas: Human activities change ecosystems at different scales. Some changes affect local habitats, while others influence entire regions or types of ecosystems.
As populations grow, human impacts tend to affect larger areas/systems.
Changing one part of the environment can indirectly affect organisms through other earth systems (e.g., changes in land use can alter water flow and sediment that affects aquatic species).
Not all species experience environmental changes in the same way (e.g., edge-loving species thrive as forests become fragmented, while interior species decline).
Change is inevitable, but slowing rates of change can provide opportunities or species to adapt through natural mechanisms.
New technologies may improve comfort, or convenience, but require new resources.
While improving efficiency of technologies decreases impact of the technology, the net effects of emerging technologies are often greater consumption as use increases.
Conservation practices can reduce negative impacts as well as use natural mechanisms or processes derived from natural processes to lessen human impacts and long-term effects.
commonStudentIdeas: Human impacts only occur through direct contact with living things, not through indirect changes.
Activities that benefit humans, benefit all species.
All species respond to changes in the same/similar ways.
Conservation actions should be expected to completely fix a problem.
Since technologies can become more efficient, they will always eventually reduce human impacts.
Extinctions happen when one species "beats" another, not because environments change faster than species can adapt.
It's always a good thing to produce conditions and benefit a species (ignores risk of benefitting invasives or reducing biodiversity).
